analysis.one_liner: Waives federal royalties on natural gas from deep wells drilled in shallow Gulf waters.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have told the Interior Department to suspend — that is, waive — the royalties that gas companies pay the federal government for natural gas they pump from deep wells under shallow Gulf of Mexico waters. Companies drilling wells at least 15,000 feet deep on old leases would get to sell 15 to 35 billion cubic feet of gas per well without paying royalties, plus relief even for up to two dry holes per tract. The relief would shut off automatically if average natural gas prices stayed above $5 per million Btu for a full year.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies holding pre-2001 federal leases in the shallow western Gulf of Mexico would keep the royalty payments on deep-well gas — money that otherwise goes to the federal Treasury — which lowers their cost of drilling expensive deep wells.

how_it_helps.text: Companies drilling successful deep wells (15,000 feet or deeper) would get royalty-free sales of 15–35 billion cubic feet of gas per well, depending on depth, with relief even for up to two dry wells per tract [S3].
The stated purpose was to speed up exploration and production of deep gas under shallow Gulf waters and to encourage new deep-drilling technology [S3].

The bill included a safeguard: the relief would stop if the average annual NYMEX natural gas price exceeded $5 per million Btu (inflation-adjusted from 2000) for a full calendar year, so the subsidy would not flow when prices were already high [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers and the Treasury, through royalty revenue forgone on gas produced from federal offshore leases.

drawbacks.text: The bill waives royalties the public is owed for gas taken from federal submerged lands, a direct transfer of public revenue to leaseholders [S2] [S3].
It applies retroactively in effect to leases issued before 2001, rewarding companies for drilling they might pursue anyway on leases they already hold [S3].
It even grants royalty relief for unsuccessful wells, so companies could collect relief on dry holes before any gas reaches the market [S3].
Its main public benefit — more gas supply — is indirect and uncertain, and the price trigger could make the whole program moot exactly when drilling incentives are most valuable to producers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a certain, measurable public cost — forgone royalties on federal gas — for an uncertain public benefit in future gas supply. The $5 price cap is a genuine safeguard against paying the subsidy during price spikes, but the core trade remains: companies that already hold the leases get public money to drill deeper, and dry-hole relief means some of that money buys nothing for consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher John, a Louisiana Democrat, introduced the bill on April 2, 2003 [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Resources the day it was introduced, and on April 10, 2003 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the bill's action history for the rest of the 108th Congress, which ended January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers came out ahead: the royalty revenue on deep Gulf gas was never waived. Gulf producers who would have received the relief did not get it, and no public subsidy for dry holes was paid.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers who kept the royalties

for.name: Rep. Christopher John
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to grant royalty relief for deep gas wells in the shallow Gulf of Mexico.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a vote, so no positions beyond the Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor are on the record; opposition came only from inaction, as the Resources Committee leadership never moved it.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers (shallow-water Gulf of Mexico)
industries.note: The bill would have waived federal royalties on their deep-well gas — public revenue converted into producer profit. Because the bill died, they kept paying royalties on leases issued before 2001.

Consumers would only have benefited indirectly if the royalty incentive actually produced more deep gas; the bill's death leaves them no worse off than before, since relief was barred anyway when prices exceeded $5 per million Btu.
